records.old: PART A — Blood Typing Simulation (35 minutes): Groups of 4 receive a simulation kit prepared by the teacher: 4 small transparent cups labelled 'Patient Sample A', 'Patient Sample B', 'Patient Sample AB', 'Patient Sample O'; two dropper bottles labelled 'Anti-A Serum' (blue food colouring in water) and 'Anti-B Serum' (red food colouring in water); a white paper backing sheet; a results recording table. The 'patient blood samples' are pre-prepared by the teacher using a colour-mixing code: Sample A = slightly yellow water; Sample B = slightly green water; Sample AB = slightly orange water; Sample O = clear water. The Anti-A serum (blue) reacts visibly only with Sample A and AB (turns them a distinct blue-green or blue-orange). The Anti-B serum (red) reacts visibly only with Sample B and AB (turns them red-green or red-orange). Sample O shows no colour change with either serum. Learners follow a step-by-step observation card: add 3 drops of Anti-A to each sample, observe and record; then add 3 drops of Anti-B to each sample, observe and record. They use their results table to determine the blood group of each sample. PART B — Kenyan Blood Group Distribution Data (10 minutes): Each group receives a data card showing estimated Kenyan blood group distribution (Blood Group O: ~46%, A: ~27%, B: ~20%, AB: ~7%, sourced from KNBTS public data). Learners draw a bar chart of the distribution on graph paper provided. PART C — Rhesus Factor Mini-Reading (5 minutes): Learners read a 150-word structured passage (on their observation card) explaining Rh+ and Rh− designations, that approximately 94% of Kenyans are Rh+, and that Rh− blood is rare and critical to stock in blood banks. They annotate two key facts.
records.new: PART A — Blood Typing Simulation (15 minutes): Groups of 4 receive a simulation kit prepared by the teacher: 4 small transparent cups labelled 'Patient Sample A', 'Patient Sample B', 'Patient Sample AB', 'Patient Sample O' (with a second cup or a plate with two spots for each sample, so that each test uses a fresh portion); two dropper bottles labelled 'Anti-A Serum' (vinegar) and 'Anti-B Serum' (iodine solution diluted to a pale tea colour); a results recording table. The teacher prepares the 'patient blood samples' in advance so that each carries a hidden 'antigen': Sample A = a quarter teaspoon of baking soda stirred into half a cup of water; Sample B = a teaspoon of cornflour (or any starch) stirred into half a cup of water; Sample AB = both of these in the same cup; Sample O = plain water. The Anti-A serum (vinegar) reacts visibly only with samples that carry the A marker (baking soda): Samples A and AB fizz. The Anti-B serum (iodine) reacts visibly only with samples that carry the B marker (starch): Samples B and AB turn blue-black. Sample O shows no reaction with either serum. Learners follow a step-by-step observation card: add 3 drops of Anti-A to a portion of each sample, observe and record (fizz or no fizz); then add 3 drops of Anti-B to a fresh portion of each sample, observe and record (only a deep blue-black counts as a reaction; the pale yellow-brown tint of the iodine itself does not). They use their results table to determine the blood group of each sample. (Teacher note: test the kit before the lesson. This is an analogue of the match between antigen and antibody: a visible reaction happens only when the 'serum' matches the hidden marker. Real agglutination is red blood cells clumping together, which this model does not show.) PART B — Kenyan Blood Group Distribution Data (7 minutes): Each group receives a data card showing estimated Kenyan blood group distribution (Blood Group O: ~46%, A: ~27%, B: ~20%, AB: ~7%, sourced from KNBTS public data). Learners draw a bar chart of the distribution on graph paper provided. PART C — Rhesus Factor Mini-Reading (7 minutes): Learners read a structured passage of about 150 words (on their observation card) explaining Rh+ and Rh− designations: red cells of Rh+ people carry the Rh (D) antigen and those of Rh− people do not; an Rh− person has no anti-D antibodies until exposed to Rh+ blood (for example in a transfusion error, or when an Rh− mother carries an Rh+ baby), after which the immune system can make anti-D that attacks Rh+ red cells later, so Rh− patients are given Rh− blood. The card also states that approximately 94% of Kenyans are Rh+ and that Rh− blood is rare and critical to stock in blood banks. They annotate two key facts.
records.why: Problems found: (1) Clear water with blue or red dye added is not 'no colour change', so Sample O could not show 'no reaction', and 'blue plus yellow' colour mixing only tests colour-mixing, not a hidden marker. (2) The reflection suggested different colours from the lesson. (3) 35 + 10 + 5 = 50 minutes of Observe left no room in an 80-minute double period. (4) KICD outcome (e) says 'explain the ABO and rhesus factor blood grouping systems' but Rhesus was a 5-minute reading of facts with no explanation. The rebuilt kit gives each sample a hidden marker and a matching 'serum' (vinegar fizzes with baking soda; iodine turns starch blue-black), so only the matching serum reacts. Check: vinegar is acetic acid, baking soda is sodium bicarbonate, they give carbon dioxide gas; iodine with starch gives a blue-black complex. The Rhesus reading now explains the antigen and anti-D idea. Teacher decision: check that vinegar, baking soda, starch and dilute iodine (or pharmacy povidone iodine) are available and test the kit once; a milder alternative is to keep the original colour kit but add a note that it only shows colour mixing.
records.reference: Royal Society of Chemistry / Nuffield classic practicals: iodine test for starch (blue-black) and acid with bicarbonate (carbon dioxide fizz); Dean L., 'Blood Groups and Red Cell Antigens', NCBI Bookshelf 2005 (ABO and Rh systems)

value.title: Part 1: Why Transport Systems Are Needed
value.prompt: Eliud Kipchoge's heart rate falls from over 170 beats per minute to about 100 within four minutes of finishing a race (an illustrative curve), and his resting rate is about 37 beats per minute. Compare this with your own pulse recovery data after star jumps. (a) Using your SA:V cube investigation (cubes with 1 cm, 2 cm and 3 cm sides), calculate the SA:V ratio of each cube and explain what happens to the ratio as an organism gets bigger. (b) Explain why diffusion alone could not supply Kipchoge's deep muscle cells during a marathon. (c) List four jobs that a transport system does in a large, active animal.
value.exemplar: (a) The 1 cm cube has a surface area of 6 cm² and a volume of 1 cm³, so SA:V = 6:1. The 2 cm cube has a surface area of 24 cm² and a volume of 8 cm³, so SA:V = 3:1. The 3 cm cube has a surface area of 54 cm² and a volume of 27 cm³, so SA:V = 2:1. As the cubes got bigger, their volume increased faster than their surface area, so the SA:V ratio fell. A larger body therefore has a smaller share of surface available for exchange compared with the volume that needs supplying. (b) Kipchoge's body is large, and his quadriceps muscle cells lie centimetres from any surface. Diffusion is too slow over such distances, so it could not deliver oxygen and nutrients or remove CO2 fast enough to sustain marathon pace. A tiny organism like an amoeba has a high SA:V and can exchange substances directly through its membrane. (c) Any four of: delivering oxygen and nutrients to all cells; removing wastes such as CO2 and urea; transporting hormones; regulating body temperature; circulating immune cells. These needs rise sharply during exercise, as our pulse and breathing data showed.

value.title: Part 2: Open and Closed Systems – The Grasshopper
value.prompt: Think about the grasshopper on the school fence. (a) Describe how its circulatory system works, naming the dorsal vessel, ostia, haemocoel and haemolymph. (b) Does haemolymph carry oxygen? Explain how the grasshopper gets oxygen to its cells. (c) Why can the grasshopper survive with this system while a large, fast-moving mammal could not?
value.exemplar: (a) The grasshopper has an open circulatory system. The dorsal vessel along its back acts as a simple pump. Haemolymph enters through small openings called ostia and floods the open body cavity (haemocoel), bathing the organs directly. There are no vessels branching to individual organs, and the haemolymph is pale yellow-green, not red. (b) No. Haemolymph does not carry oxygen. Oxygen is delivered directly to cells by a separate tracheal system. (c) The grasshopper is small, so diffusion distances are short, and its tracheae supply oxygen without needing the circulatory system. Its open system works at low pressure and cannot direct oxygen-rich fluid to particular muscles on demand. A large, active mammal needs a high-pressure closed system to do this.

value.title: Part 3: Comparing Hearts – Tilapia, Frog and Mammal
value.prompt: Compare the heart and circulation of the tilapia from Lake Victoria, the frog from the Rift Valley wetlands, and a mammal such as Kipchoge. (a) Complete a table with the columns: animal, number of heart chambers, single or double circulation, and what happens to oxygenated and deoxygenated blood. (b) Explain why the tilapia's blood reaches the body with lower pressure than blood in a mammal. (c) Explain why a frog's body tissues receive only partly oxygenated blood, and why this trade-off is acceptable for a frog but not for Kipchoge.
value.exemplar:
(a) | Animal | Heart chambers | Circulation | Blood separation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Tilapia | Two (one atrium, one ventricle) | Single, closed | Heart to gills to body to heart; one loop |
| Frog | Three (two atria, one ventricle) | Double, but ventricle shared | Oxygenated and deoxygenated blood mix in the single ventricle |
| Mammal (Kipchoge) | Four | Double, closed | Complete separation by the septum; no mixing |
(b) In the tilapia, blood passes through two sets of capillaries (gills, then body) before returning to the heart. Pressure drops after the gill capillaries and the blood is not pumped again, so delivery to body tissues is less forceful. In a mammal, the left ventricle re-pressurises oxygenated blood before it goes to the body. (c) In the frog, oxygenated blood from the lungs and deoxygenated blood from the body (including blood from the skin, which returns to the right atrium) mix partly in the single ventricle, so tissues receive partly oxygenated blood. This is acceptable because frogs are ectotherms with lower energy demands. Kipchoge has very high, sustained oxygen demand, so he needs a four-chambered heart that delivers fully oxygenated blood.

value.title: Part 4: The Mammalian Heart and Kipchoge's Recovery
value.prompt: Use your sheep or goat heart observations and your pulse-rate data. (a) Describe two structural features of the mammalian heart and say what each does. (b) Explain what the sino-atrial node (SAN) does and what causes the 'lub-dub' sounds. (c) Kipchoge's heart rate is about 37 beats per minute at rest, yet each beat pumps about 135 mL, compared with about 67 mL for an average person. Explain how these figures allow his resting heart rate to be so low. Then use your pulse-rate recovery data and the Lesson 1 curves to describe how his heart rate changes after a race, and suggest what in the control of his heart rate could account for how quickly it returns to rest.
value.exemplar: (a) Any two: a thick muscular septum separates the left and right sides so oxygenated and deoxygenated blood do not mix; the left ventricle wall is thicker than the right, giving enough force to pump blood around the whole body; valves between atria and ventricles prevent backflow; coronary vessels on the outside supply the heart muscle itself. (b) The SAN, in the right atrial wall, generates the electrical impulse that starts each heartbeat, so it is the heart's pacemaker. The 'lub' is the closing of the bicuspid and tricuspid valves at the start of ventricular systole; the 'dub' is the closing of the semi-lunar valves at its end. (c) Cardiac output is heart rate multiplied by stroke volume. Because each beat of Kipchoge's trained ventricles pumps about 135 mL, nearly double the roughly 67 mL of an average person, he needs only about 37 beats per minute to deliver the same blood volume per minute at rest. This large stroke volume explains his low resting rate, but it does not by itself explain how fast he recovers. After a race his heart rate falls from over 170 beats per minute to about 100 within four minutes on the Lesson 1 curve, much faster than our own pulse recovered, and keeps falling towards his low resting baseline. The speed of this fall is a matter of how the SAN's firing rate is controlled: adrenaline speeds the SAN up during the race, and once exercise stops, nerve signals that slow the SAN take over again, so the rate drops quickly; his well-trained muscles also need less extra oxygen, so less extra pumping is needed. The large stroke volume explains the low resting rate the heart settles towards, but not by itself the speed of the fall. The details of how that control works were not investigated in our lessons, so this remains a reasoned suggestion rather than something we measured.

value.title: Part 5: Blood, Defence and Compatibility
value.prompt: (a) Explain how the lymphatic system supports the blood circulatory system, and why a person's legs swell (oedema) when lymph vessels are blocked, for example in lymphatic filariasis. (b) Put the main steps of blood clotting after a cut in order, and state one difference between non-specific and specific immunity. (c) A patient with blood group B Rh-negative needs a transfusion. Using your compatibility matrix, state which donor groups could safely be used, and explain why blood group O Rh-negative is kept in blood banks for emergencies.
value.exemplar: (a) Blood capillaries leak plasma into the tissue spaces, forming tissue fluid. Lymph capillaries absorb the excess, which is then called lymph, and lymph vessels with valves carry it through lymph nodes, which filter pathogens, to the thoracic duct and right lymphatic duct, which return it to the blood at the subclavian veins. If lymph vessels are blocked, for example by filarial worms, fluid cannot drain back, so it builds up in the tissues and the legs swell (oedema). (b) Injury damages the vessel wall; platelets gather at the wound and form a plug; clotting factors are activated and convert prothrombin to thrombin; thrombin converts soluble fibrinogen to insoluble fibrin; the fibrin mesh traps red blood cells and forms the clot. Non-specific immunity (for example phagocytes engulfing bacteria) responds quickly to many kinds of germ and forms no memory; specific immunity (lymphocytes making antibodies) targets one germ and forms memory cells, so the second response is faster. (c) A patient with group B has anti-A antibodies, so can receive group B or group O red cells. Being Rh-negative, the patient should receive Rh-negative blood, because Rh-positive blood can make the patient form anti-D antibodies. Suitable donors are B Rh-negative or O Rh-negative. O Rh-negative red cells carry no A, B or Rh antigens, so they can be given to almost any patient in an emergency when the blood group is not yet known.

value.title: Part 6: Final Explanation (CER)
value.prompt: Answer the driving question using CER. Claim: how does the structure of an animal's transport system determine its ability to survive and thrive? Evidence: give at least three pieces of evidence from different lessons, naming the animals. Reasoning: explain how the evidence supports your claim. Then explain what would happen if Eliud Kipchoge had the circulatory system of a grasshopper. Finally, say how your final model differs from your Lesson 1 model.
value.exemplar: Claim: The structure of an animal's transport system determines how well it can meet its oxygen and nutrient demands, so it sets the level of activity the animal can sustain. Evidence: (1) The grasshopper has an open system with haemolymph that does not carry oxygen, and tracheae deliver oxygen directly, which suits its small size and low demand. (2) The tilapia has a closed, single circulation with a two-chambered heart, and pressure drops after the gills. (3) The frog's three-chambered heart mixes oxygenated and deoxygenated blood. (4) Kipchoge's four-chambered heart with double circulation keeps the blood fully separated, and his large stroke volume (about 135 mL) lets his heart rate be about 37 beats per minute at rest. Reasoning: Across the animals, circulation becomes more complex: open to closed, single to double, and mixed to fully separated blood. Each step improves oxygen delivery per heartbeat and matches the animal's energy demand. Kipchoge's size and muscle demand are very high, so he needs the most efficient system. If he had a grasshopper's system, he is far too large for diffusion and low-pressure haemolymph to supply his leg muscles, and haemolymph does not carry oxygen. The system could not direct oxygen-rich fluid to working muscles on demand, so his muscles would fail quickly at marathon pace. Without a high-pressure closed system with a powerful heart and SAN, he would also lack the means to meet his body's demand and bring his heart rate down quickly after the race towards his resting rate of about 37 beats per minute. Model change: My Lesson 1 sketch was a rough guess at a transport system. My final model shows open and closed systems, the heart chambers of each animal, the path of blood in the double circuit, and the SAN, with evidence labels.

A new Part 5, 'Blood, Defence and Compatibility', with a worked answer key, assesses them; the CER part becomes Part 6 and stays the culminating task. Answer check: blood group B has anti-A antibodies so can take B or O red cells; an Rh-negative patient should receive Rh-negative blood; so suitable donors are B- or O-; O-negative cells carry no A, B or Rh antigens.

value.criterion: Explaining why transport systems are needed
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Links SA:V ratio, diffusion distance and the functions of transport accurately, using the cube and pulse data.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Explains that large animals need transport and names some functions, with limited use of SA:V evidence.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: States that animals need transport without a clear reason or evidence.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Accurately compares grasshopper, tilapia, frog and mammal on open or closed, single or double, and mixing of blood, using correct terms.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Describes most systems correctly with a few gaps or errors.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Describes few systems, or confuses their features.

value.criterion: Explaining lymph, immunity, clotting and blood groups
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Accurately explains how lymph returns tissue fluid, orders the clotting steps, distinguishes non-specific from specific immunity, and applies the ABO and Rhesus rules to choose a safe donor, giving reasons.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Explains most of these ideas correctly with minor gaps, and chooses a safe donor group.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Names some of these ideas but gives few reasons, or chooses an unsafe donor.

value.criterion: Use of evidence and CER reasoning
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Gives at least three accurate pieces of evidence from different lessons and links each clearly to the claim.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Gives two or three pieces of evidence with partial reasoning.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Gives little or vague evidence; claim is not supported.

value.criterion: Applying ideas to Kipchoge and the grasshopper scenario
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Explains fully why a grasshopper system would fail Kipchoge, covering size, pressure, oxygen carrying and recovery, using the heart rate and stroke volume data.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Explains that the system would not supply enough oxygen, with some reasons.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Gives an unsupported or incorrect prediction.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Uses scientific vocabulary precisely and clearly describes how the final model differs from the Lesson 1 model.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Uses mostly correct vocabulary and names some changes to the model.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Vocabulary is often incorrect and model changes are not described.
